The '''Mott–Schottky equation''' relates the [[capacitance]] to the applied [[potential|voltage]] across a [[semiconductor]]-[[electrolyte]] [[electrical junction|junction]].<ref>{{cite journal |last=Gelderman |first=K. |title=Flat-Band Potential of a Semiconductor: Using the Mott–Schottky Equation |journal=[[Journal of Chemical Education]] |volume=84 |pages=685 |year=2007 |issue=4 | doi=10.1021/ed084p685|bibcode=2007JChEd..84..685G }}</ref>

<math>\frac{1}{C^2} = \frac{2}{\epsilon \epsilon_0 A^2 e N_d} (V - V_{fb} - \frac{k_B T}{e})</math>

where <math>C</math> is the differential capacitance <math>\frac{\partial{Q}}{\partial{V}}</math>, <math>\epsilon</math> is the [[dielectric constant]] of the semiconductor, <math>\epsilon_0</math> is the [[permittivity of free space]], <math>A</math> is the area such that the [[depletion region]] volume is <math>w A</math>, <math>e</math> is the elementary charge, <math>N_d</math> is the density of dopants, <math>V</math> is the applied potential, <math>V_{fb}</math> is the [[flat band potential]], <math>k_B</math> is the [[Boltzmann constant]], and T is the [[absolute temperature]].

This theory predicts that a [[Mott–Schottky plot]] will be linear.  The doping density <math>N_d</math> can be derived from the slope of the plot (provided the area and dielectric constant are known).  The flatband potential can be determined as well; absent the temperature term, the plot would cross the <math>V</math>-axis at the flatband potential.

==Derivation==
Under an applied potential <math>V</math>, the width of the depletion region is<ref name=Grundmann/>

<math>w = (\frac{2 \epsilon \epsilon_0}{e N_d} ( V - V_{fb} ) )^\frac{1}{2}</math>

Using the [[abrupt approximation]],<ref name=Grundmann>{{cite book|author1-link=Marius Grundmann |last=Grundmann | first=Marius | title=The Physics of Semiconductors | section=Section 20.2.2 | publisher=Springer | year=2010 | isbn=978-3-642-13883-6}}</ref> all charge carriers except the ionized dopants have left the depletion region, so the charge density in the depletion region is <math>e N_d</math>, and the total charge of the depletion region, compensated by opposite charge nearby in the electrolyte, is

<math>Q = e N_d A w = e N_d A (\frac{2 \epsilon \epsilon_0}{e N_d} ( V - V_{fb} ) )^\frac{1}{2}</math>

Thus, the differential capacitance is

<math>C = \frac{\partial{Q}}{\partial{V}} = e N_d A \frac{1}{2}(\frac{2 \epsilon \epsilon_0}{e N_d})^\frac{1}{2}
      ( V - V_{fb} )^{-\frac{1}{2}} = A (\frac{e N_d \epsilon \epsilon_0}{2(V - V_{fb})})^\frac{1}{2}</math>

which is equivalent to the Mott-Schottky equation, save for the temperature term.  In fact the temperature term arises from a more careful analysis, which takes [[statistical mechanics]] into account by abandoning the abrupt approximation and solving the [[Poisson–Boltzmann equation]] for the charge density in the depletion region.<ref name=Grundmann/>
